cards.f: If you can't tell whether a new problem is Subsets, Combinations, or Permutations, what's the fastest way to check?
cards.b: Write out the decision tree by hand for a size-3 example before writing any code.

cards.f: How does Combination Sum III differ from plain Combinations?
cards.b: It adds a target-sum constraint (like Combination Sum) on top of the fixed-count, no-reuse structure of Combinations, with candidates restricted to `1..9`.

cards.f: What makes Target Sum a binary-decision (Pattern A) problem despite not building a `path`?
cards.b: Each number gets exactly 2 choices (add it or subtract it into a running total) -- structurally identical to take/skip, just accumulating a sum instead of a list.

cards.f: What two prunes make Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets tractable?
cards.b: Sorting descending (fail fast on oversized elements) and skipping a duplicate value whose identical predecessor wasn't used yet (same-level dedup, applied to "which element starts a new group").

cards.f: How is Beautiful Arrangement structurally identical to Permutations?
cards.b: Same `used[]` + choose-any-unused-value structure; it just adds one extra validity check (`perm[i] % i == 0 or i % perm[i] == 0`) before committing each choice.

cards.f: In Word Pattern II, what must be kept in sync as two separate maps, and why?
cards.b: `char_to_word` and `word_to_char`, both updated and undone together -- enforcing that the mapping between pattern characters and substrings is a true bijection (no two pattern characters share a substring).

cards.f: What's the key trick behind Generalized Abbreviation's recursion?
cards.b: A binary decision at each character -- extend a numeric "run" (abbreviate) or flush the run and keep the character literally -- with careful bookkeeping of when the run must be flushed.

cards.f: Why does Palindrome Permutation II only need to permute half the character multiset?
cards.b: A palindrome mirrors around its center; once you fix at most one odd-count character as the middle, the first half fully determines the second half.

cards.f: What problem does a Trie solve that a HashSet doesn't?
cards.b: A HashSet answers "does this exact word exist?" but can't efficiently answer "does any word start with this prefix?" A Trie makes shared prefixes a physical path, so prefix queries are O(L) instead of scanning every word.

cards.f: What does the "root" of a Trie represent?
cards.b: The starting point / the empty string. It does not represent a character itself.

cards.f: What does an edge in a Trie represent?
cards.b: One character transition from one node to the next.

cards.f: What does a path from the root to a node represent?
cards.b: A string/prefix — the characters along the edges, in order.

cards.f: What two fields does a minimal TrieNode need?
cards.b: `children` (map from character to next TrieNode) and `is_end` (whether a complete word ends at this node).

cards.f: Why can't we tell if a word was inserted just by checking that its path exists in the Trie?
cards.b: The path existing only means some longer word passes through it (it's a valid prefix). Only `is_end == True` at the final node confirms the exact word was itself inserted.

cards.f: After inserting only "care", what are `node("car").is_end` and `node("care").is_end`?
cards.b: `node("car").is_end = False` (never inserted as its own word), `node("care").is_end = True`.

cards.f: If we then also insert "car" into a Trie that already has "care", does that create new nodes for c, a, r?
cards.b: No — c, a, r already exist on the path to "care", so they're reused. Only `is_end` at the r node changes, from False to True.

cards.f: What is the fundamental rule distinguishing exact-word lookup from prefix lookup in a Trie?
cards.b: Exact word: path exists AND `is_end == True`. Prefix: path exists (is_end is irrelevant).

cards.f: In a Trie built from only "apple" and "application", what do `search("app")` and `startsWith("app")` return, and why?
cards.b: `search("app") == False` (no word "app" was ever inserted) but `startsWith("app") == True` (the path exists — both words pass through the "app" node).

cards.f: A quiz question asked whether checking if the prefix "ca" exists (Trie built from cat/car/care) needs to check is_end. What's the correct answer and the common wrong reasoning?
cards.b: Correct answer: No — prefix existence needs only the path, never is_end. A common wrong instinct answers based on which letters the stored words happen to end with, rather than recognizing that search() and startsWith() are simply different questions about the same node.

cards.f: What are the three core Trie operations from the source lesson?
cards.b: `insert(word)`, `search(word)`, `startsWith(prefix)`.

cards.f: Describe the insert algorithm in one sentence.
cards.b: Walk the word character by character, creating a child node whenever one doesn't already exist, then set `is_end = True` on the final node.

cards.f: Describe the search algorithm in one sentence.
cards.b: Walk the word character by character, returning False immediately if any child is missing; if the full word is walked, return `is_end` at the final node.

cards.f: Describe the startsWith algorithm in one sentence.
cards.b: Walk the prefix character by character, returning False immediately if any child is missing; if the full prefix is walked, return True (no is_end check).

cards.f: What is the time complexity of insert/search/startsWith, in terms of L = word/prefix length?
cards.b: O(L) for all three — never O(1), and never proportional to the number of stored words.

cards.f: What is the space complexity of a Trie storing many words with shared prefixes?
cards.b: O(total number of unique character positions after prefix sharing) — not the sum of every word's raw length, since shared prefixes are stored once.

cards.f: Insert "cat" into an empty Trie, then "car". How many total new nodes are created?
cards.b: 4 new nodes for "cat" (c, a, t, but root already existed — actually c,a,t = 3 new), then only 1 new node (r) for "car" since c and a are reused. Total 4 new nodes beyond root.

cards.f: What are the two stages of an autocomplete algorithm built on a Trie?
cards.b: 1) Walk to the node representing the prefix. 2) DFS/BFS from that node, collecting every descendant where `is_end == True`.

cards.f: In autocomplete, does the Trie directly return the list of completions?
cards.b: No — it only gives the correct starting point (the prefix node). DFS from there does the actual work of finding complete words.

cards.f: Given a Trie with app, apple, application, apt all stored, and you're standing at the "app" node during DFS — what tells you "the path built so far is a complete word, add it to results"?
cards.b: `node.is_end == True`.

cards.f: What is the time complexity of autocomplete(prefix), in terms of P = prefix length and K = total characters explored/returned?
cards.b: O(P + K) — proportional to the prefix length plus the output size, not to the total dictionary size.

cards.f: In LC 211 (Add and Search Words), what does a '.' character mean during search?
cards.b: It matches any single character — try every existing child at that position.

cards.f: What's the key rule change wildcard search introduces vs. plain Trie search?
cards.b: Normal character: follow exactly one child. Wildcard '.': try every existing child and recurse (DFS) — one path becomes multiple possible paths.

cards.f: What is the worst-case time complexity of WordDictionary.search with L wildcards over a 26-letter alphabet?
cards.b: O(26^L) in the worst case (a pattern of all dots), since every wildcard position can branch into up to 26 children.

cards.f: Why is WordDictionary's search described as "Trie + DFS/backtracking" rather than just "Trie traversal"?
cards.b: Because a wildcard forces trying multiple children and recursively continuing each possibility — that's a DFS/backtracking search over branching paths, not a single deterministic walk.

cards.f: In Word Search II, why do we build a Trie from the dictionary before doing board DFS?
cards.b: So that at every step of board DFS, we can check in O(1) whether the current partial string is still a valid prefix of some dictionary word — instantly pruning branches that can't possibly lead to a match.

cards.f: What's the core recognition pattern behind Word Search II?
cards.b: Backtracking generates candidate strings; the Trie kills impossible candidates the instant they stop being a valid prefix. Backtracking + Trie = prefix-pruned search.

cards.f: In an implementation of findWords, why reset a terminal node's is_end after collecting its word?
cards.b: To avoid re-adding the same word to the results if a different board path reaches the same Trie node again.

cards.f: In an implementation of findWords, why delete a Trie node from its parent's children once it has no children left?
cards.b: A dead-end node (no children, its word already collected) can never contribute a match again — leaving it wastes time on every future DFS call that walks into that branch.

cards.f: In Replace Words, what should replace each sentence word?
cards.b: The shortest dictionary word that is a prefix of it (its "root").

cards.f: How do you find the shortest matching dictionary prefix using a Trie?
cards.b: Walk the word through the Trie left to right; the FIRST node where `is_end == True` gives the shortest prefix — stop immediately, don't keep walking.

cards.f: Why does walking left-to-right and stopping at the first is_end guarantee the SHORTEST matching prefix?
cards.b: Because prefixes get longer as you walk further right; the first one you hit that's a complete word is necessarily the shortest possible match.

cards.f: What extra information does MapSum store at each Trie node, beyond children/is_end?
cards.b: A running `total` — the sum of values of every inserted key whose path passes through this node.

cards.f: In MapSum, if you insert("apple", 3) and later insert("apple", 10), why can't you just add 10 to every node's total?
cards.b: That would double-count the original 3. You must compute the delta (10 - 3 = 7) and add only the delta to every node on the key's path.

cards.f: What is the time complexity of MapSum.sum(prefix) once nodes store running totals?
cards.b: O(len(prefix)) — no DFS needed, since the sum is already precomputed at that node.

cards.f: What general Trie technique does Map Sum Pairs demonstrate?
cards.b: That a Trie node can be augmented with arbitrary extra bookkeeping (not just children/is_end) to answer richer queries efficiently.

cards.f: What is the key insight for maximizing nums[i] XOR nums[j] using a Trie?
cards.b: XOR wants bits to differ (0 XOR 1 = 1 XOR 0 = 1), so at every bit position you should prefer the OPPOSITE bit of the current number — this bit-by-bit branching structure is naturally a Trie, just over bits instead of letters.

cards.f: Why does a Trie for Maximum XOR insert numbers bit-by-bit from most-significant to least-significant?
cards.b: Because the greedy query must make its highest-impact decision first — the highest bit position contributes the most to the final XOR value, so it must be decided before lower bits.

cards.f: What is the time complexity of findMaximumXOR using a binary Trie, for N numbers with B-bit width?
cards.b: O(N·B) = O(N) for fixed-width integers — much better than the naive O(N^2) all-pairs comparison.

cards.f: What broader lesson does the binary Trie (Max XOR) teach about Tries in general?
cards.b: A Trie isn't fundamentally about letters — it's about navigating a branching sequence of choices. The choices can be characters, or bits, or anything with a fixed set of options at each step.

cards.f: In LC 720, what extra condition must a word satisfy beyond just being in the dictionary to be a candidate answer?
cards.b: Every one of its prefixes must ALSO be a stored word (e.g. "world" qualifies only if w, wo, wor, worl, world are all individually stored).

cards.f: How does the DFS in longestWord differ from a normal Trie DFS?
cards.b: It may only step into a child if that child's `is_end` is already True — if a node isn't itself a complete word, its whole subtree is unreachable, since some prefix along that path was never a complete word.

cards.f: In longestWord, given words including "banana", "ban", "bana" but NOT "banan" — can "banana" be reached by the DFS?
cards.b: No — DFS reaches "bana" but "bana" has no is_end child leading toward "banan" (never inserted), so the branch toward "banana" is pruned before it's reached.

cards.f: How does a Trie help with the classic Word Break problem (can string s be segmented into dictionary words)?
cards.b: At each starting index i, walk the Trie through s[i], s[i+1], ... — whenever a node has is_end == True, you've found a candidate word boundary, and then check (via DP) whether the remainder can also be segmented.

cards.f: What combination of techniques solves Word Break using a Trie?
cards.b: Trie + DP — the Trie incrementally finds valid word boundaries character by character; DP combines those boundaries into a full-string segmentation answer.

cards.f: What's the time complexity of the Trie + DP Word Break approach, for string length n and max dictionary word length L?
cards.b: O(n·L) time, O(n) extra space for the DP array (plus the Trie's own space).

cards.f: What problem does LC 745 (Prefix and Suffix Search) solve that a plain Trie can't?
cards.b: It needs BOTH a prefix and a suffix to match simultaneously — an ordinary Trie only answers prefix questions.

cards.f: What's the trick behind WordFilter's combined-Trie approach?
cards.b: Index every (suffix, whole word) combination as one string `suffix + '#' + word` in a single shared Trie. A query walks `suffix + '#' + prefix` through that same Trie — a surviving path guarantees both the prefix and suffix match.

cards.f: In WordFilter, what does each Trie node additionally store, and why?
cards.b: The largest word index that passed through it during insertion, so a successful query walk ends exactly at the answer (the highest-indexed matching word).

cards.f: What two things does LC 642 (Autocomplete System) combine?
cards.b: The Trie + DFS autocomplete pattern (find every sentence matching the typed prefix) plus a ranking rule — sort matches by (highest frequency first, then lexicographically) and return the top 3.

cards.f: What extra field does each Trie node track in AutocompleteSystem, beyond is_end?
cards.b: A `count` — incremented every time a sentence is typed to completion (from initial history or when the user finishes typing with '#').

cards.f: What two counters does each node track in Implement Trie II, instead of a boolean is_end?
cards.b: `word_count` (how many times this exact word was inserted) and `prefix_count` (how many inserted words pass through this node at all).

cards.f: How does erase(word) work in Trie II?
cards.b: Walk the same path used by insert, decrementing prefix_count on every node along the path and word_count on the final node.

cards.f: What's the first question to ask when deciding whether a problem needs a Trie?
cards.b: Are we dealing with sequences/strings (or bits) at all? If no, a Trie is probably irrelevant.

cards.f: When should you prefer a HashSet/HashMap over a Trie?
cards.b: When you only need exact membership or key->value lookup, with no prefix structure involved — a HashSet is simpler and often just as fast for that.

cards.f: What signal in a problem statement suggests "Trie + DFS/backtracking" rather than plain Trie traversal?
cards.b: Wildcards (any-character matches) or backtracking through strings/grids that needs incremental prefix validity checks.

cards.f: List the four Trie pattern categories worth memorizing.
cards.b: 1) Trie traversal (insert/search/startsWith). 2) Trie + DFS (autocomplete, wildcards, dictionary collection). 3) Trie + backtracking (prefix pruning, e.g. Word Search II). 4) Trie + another algorithm (Trie + DP for Word Break, binary Trie + greedy for Max XOR).

cards.f: Why is a Trie NOT automatically better than a HashSet?
cards.b: A Trie can use significantly more memory, since every character transition may require its own node and child references — worth it only when prefix structure genuinely matters to the problem.

cards.f: What single question captures the difference between what a HashSet and a Trie each answer?
cards.b: HashSet asks "does this exact word exist?" Trie asks "where does this prefix take me, and what can continue from here?"

cards.f: What is the central mental model for deciding which pointer to move in an opposite-end two-pointer scan?
cards.b: Don't apply a memorized rule ("sum small -> left++"). Instead prove that the current pointer's value can never be part of the answer, and only then move it.

cards.f: In Two Sum II on a sorted array, why can `nums[left]` be eliminated when `nums[left] + nums[right] < target`?
cards.b: `nums[right]` is already the largest available partner. If even that sum is too small, every other (smaller) partner for `nums[left]` is also too small, so `nums[left]` can never reach the target.

cards.f: Why can `nums[right]` be eliminated when `nums[left] + nums[right] > target`?
cards.b: `nums[left]` is already the smallest available partner. If even that sum is too large, every other (larger) partner for `nums[right]` is also too large.

cards.f: Why does sorting matter for opposite-end elimination proofs?
cards.b: Sorting creates a monotonic relationship -- moving `left` right only increases `nums[left]`, moving `right` left only decreases `nums[right]` -- which is what turns "sum too small/large" into a valid proof of impossibility.

cards.f: On `[8, 1, 6, 3, 4]` (unsorted), `8 + 1 = 9 < target`. Can we safely conclude "1 is too small, move left"?
cards.b: No. Without sorted order there's no guarantee a value like 2 or 5 doesn't exist elsewhere in the array that would work with 1.

cards.f: What is the classic self-correction: `nums=[1,2,4,7,11]`, `target=13`, `L=0,R=4`, sum=12 (too small). Why is "move R, eliminate 11" wrong?
cards.b: Eliminating 11 requires proving 11 can never be part of a valid pair, but that's false in general -- 11 could pair with something smaller than 1 elsewhere. The sum being too small only proves the LEFT value (1) is impossible.

cards.f: For `nums=[1,2,4,7,11]`, `target=13`, what is the correct first move and why?
cards.b: Move left (eliminate 1). 11 is already the largest possible partner, and 1+11=12 < 13, so 1 can never reach the target with any partner.

cards.f: What is the time and space complexity of the Two Sum II opposite-end scan?
cards.b: O(n) time (left and right together move at most n steps total) and O(1) extra space.

cards.f: What three cases does the opposite-end scan handle at each step?
cards.b: sum < target (move left), sum > target (move right), sum == target (found, stop).

cards.f: Given `nums=[1,3,5,7,10]`, `target=11`, at `L=0,R=4` we get `1+10=11`. What happens next?
cards.b: We return immediately -- a valid pair is already found, so there's nothing left to eliminate or search for.

cards.f: What is the area formula in Container With Most Water?
cards.b: `min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)`.

cards.f: Why is Container With Most Water's pointer-elimination proof different in kind from Two Sum II's?
cards.b: Two Sum eliminates a VALUE because no partner can reach the target. Container eliminates a POINTER POSITION because keeping the shorter side while shrinking the width can never produce a better area -- it's an optimization proof, not a value-impossibility proof.

cards.f: If `height[left] < height[right]`, why is moving `right` provably useless?
cards.b: `left` stays the limiting (shorter) height, so the new area is at most `height[left] * smaller_width`, which is strictly less than the current area.

cards.f: If `height[left] < height[right]`, why might moving `left` help?
cards.b: It's the only move that could reveal a taller wall, which could raise the limiting height and increase the area.

cards.f: When `height[left] == height[right]`, which pointer should move?
cards.b: Either one -- both sides are equally limiting, and the current pair's area can never be reused at a better (larger) width, so there's no reason to prefer one side.

cards.f: In Container With Most Water, when do we update the running best answer?
cards.b: Before moving either pointer, at every (left, right) pair we compute the area and update `best = max(best, area)`.

cards.f: In Valid Palindrome, why don't we need to build a cleaned copy of the string first?
cards.b: The two pointers can skip non-alphanumeric characters in place while scanning inward, comparing only the meaningful characters as they go.

cards.f: In Valid Palindrome, why can we return `False` immediately on the first mismatch?
cards.b: A palindrome requires every mirrored pair of characters to match; one violation is proof enough, so there's no need to inspect the rest.

cards.f: How does Valid Palindrome II (LC 680) extend the Valid Palindrome scan?
cards.b: On the first mismatch, try skipping the left character OR the right character and check whether either resulting substring is a clean palindrome -- one deletion is allowed.

cards.f: In Valid Palindrome II, why do we stop trying more deletions after the first mismatch?
cards.b: Only one deletion is allowed total, so once it's used (on either side), the remaining range must already be a clean, no-further-deletion palindrome.

cards.f: What pointer pattern does Reverse String (LC 344) use, and why doesn't it need an elimination proof?
cards.b: Opposite-end swap. Every position must be visited exactly once to reverse the array, so no value is ever "eliminated" -- the pointers just swap inward until they meet.

cards.f: In Is Subsequence, what do pointers `i` and `j` each represent?
cards.b: `i` = the next character of `s` we still need to match. `j` = a scanner walking through `t`.

cards.f: In Is Subsequence, why can `j` always advance even on a mismatch, but `i` cannot?
cards.b: We're allowed to delete/skip characters from `t`, so skipping `t[j]` loses nothing. But `i` has not yet found its required match, so advancing it would lose a needed character of `s`.

cards.f: What is the success condition for Is Subsequence?
cards.b: `i == len(s)` -- once every character of `s` has been consumed in order, `s` is a subsequence of `t`.

cards.f: What is the time complexity of Is Subsequence's two-pointer scan?
cards.b: O(len(t)) -- `j` scans `t` at most once, and `i` can never advance more times than `j` does.

cards.f: In the slow/fast "processed region" pattern, what do `slow` and `fast` represent in general?
cards.b: `slow` = the boundary of the region already correctly built. `fast` = a scanner searching the rest of the array for something that belongs in that region.

cards.f: In Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (LC 26), why is it enough for `fast` to compare against `nums[slow - 1]` only?
cards.b: Because the array is sorted, duplicates are always adjacent, so the single most-recently-kept value is enough to detect a repeat.

cards.f: How does Remove Duplicates II (LC 80) change the comparison rule to allow each value twice?
cards.b: Compare `fast` against `nums[slow - 2]` instead of `nums[slow - 1]`, so a value is only rejected once it would be a third consecutive occurrence.

cards.f: In Remove Element (LC 27), what does `slow` represent, and is a swap required?
cards.b: `slow` is the next destination for a value we want to keep. A swap is only one implementation detail -- the core idea is compacting kept elements toward the front.

cards.f: In Move Zeroes (LC 283), why don't we need a separate step to move zeroes to the end?
cards.b: Once every non-zero element has been placed in front (up to `slow`), nothing else is left to place, so everything from `slow` onward can simply be overwritten with 0.

cards.f: In Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag, LC 75), what do `low`, `mid`, and `high` track?
cards.b: The boundaries of four regions: `[0 region][1 region][unknown][2 region]`, with `mid` scanning the unknown region.

cards.f: In Sort Colors, why must `mid` NOT advance immediately after swapping in a value from `high` when it finds a `2`?
cards.b: The value just swapped in from `high` has never been examined -- it could be a 0, 1, or another 2, so it still needs to be checked.

cards.f: In Sort Colors, why IS it safe for `mid` to advance right after swapping in a value from `low` when it finds a `0`?
cards.b: The value swapped in from `low` is always either untouched or already known to be a `1` from earlier in the scan, so it's safe to move past it.

cards.f: How does Squares of a Sorted Array (LC 977) use two pointers, and what's different about its proof?
cards.b: It fills the answer array from the back, always taking whichever end (`left` or `right`) has the larger absolute value -- not an elimination proof about a target, but about where the largest remaining square must come from.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: What is the general recipe for solving 3Sum with two pointers?
cards.b: Sort the array, fix one index `i`, then run the Two Sum II opposite-end elimination proof on the remaining subarray.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: In 3Sum, why do we skip duplicate values of the fixed index `i`?
cards.b: Starting a full search from two indices holding the same value would just rediscover the exact same triplets.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: In 3Sum, is it correct to skip duplicate `L`/`R` values BEFORE any triplet has been found for the current `i`?
cards.b: No. A duplicate value may still be a necessary stepping stone the pointer must pass through while searching -- skipping it early could skip over a still-needed combination.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: In 3Sum, when IS it correct (and necessary) to skip duplicate `L`/`R` values?
cards.b: Only AFTER a triplet has been recorded -- moving to the next occurrence of the same value at that point is guaranteed to reproduce the same triplet, so skipping avoids duplicate output.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: What is the time complexity of 3Sum, and why?
cards.b: O(n^2) -- n choices for the fixed index `i`, times an O(n) opposite-end scan for each.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: How does 4Sum extend the 3Sum pattern, and what's its complexity?
cards.b: Fix two indices `i` and `j` instead of one, then run the same L/R elimination on what's left. Complexity is O(n^3): n^2 choices for `(i,j)` times an O(n) scan.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: How does 3Sum Closest differ from 3Sum in its stopping condition?
cards.b: Instead of stopping at an exact match, it tracks the best `abs(sum - target)` seen so far, while still moving L/R by the same too-small/too-large direction rule.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: In 3Sum Smaller, why can we count `(right - left)` triplets at once instead of one at a time?
cards.b: Once `nums[i]+nums[left]+nums[right] < target` is true, it stays true for `nums[left]` paired with every index between `left` and `right` (not just `right`), because the array is sorted.

cards.t: Sort + Fixed Pointer(s) + Two Pointers (kSum Family)
cards.f: In Valid Triangle Number (LC 611), what does fixing `nums[k]` from the right represent, and why is only one inequality checked?
cards.b: `nums[k]` is fixed as the LARGEST side. Only `nums[L] + nums[R] > nums[k]` needs checking because the other two triangle inequalities hold automatically once the array is sorted and `L, R < k`.

cards.f: In merge-style two pointers (one per sorted sequence), what does each pointer represent?
cards.b: The smallest unprocessed candidate from its own sequence.

cards.f: Why is it always safe to consume the smaller of `A[i]` and `B[j]` in a merge-style scan?
cards.b: Since both sequences are sorted, every remaining element in each array is >= its own pointer's current value, so the globally smaller of the two current values must be the next element in merged order.

cards.f: What is the time complexity of merging two sorted sequences with one pointer each?
cards.b: O(n + m) -- each pointer only ever moves forward through its own array.

cards.f: Why does Merge Sorted Array (LC 88) scan from the BACK instead of the front?
cards.b: `nums1` has trailing empty capacity to merge into; scanning from the front would overwrite values in `nums1` before they're read. Scanning from the back and taking the LARGEST unprocessed candidate each step avoids that.

cards.t: Hard Problems Requiring Their Own Proof
cards.f: In Trapping Rain Water, what does the invariant `left_max <= right_max` let us conclude?
cards.b: The water level at `left` is fully determined by `left_max` alone -- the right side is guaranteed to have a wall at least that high somewhere, so we don't need to know exactly where.

cards.t: Hard Problems Requiring Their Own Proof
cards.f: What two running values does the two-pointer Trapping Rain Water solution maintain, and what space complexity does that achieve?
cards.b: `left_max` and `right_max`; this achieves O(1) extra space instead of the O(n) prefix/suffix max arrays.

cards.t: Hard Problems Requiring Their Own Proof
cards.f: In Boats to Save People, why must the heaviest remaining person either pair with the lightest, or go alone?
cards.b: The heaviest person must go on some boat. If they can't fit with the lightest remaining person, they can't fit with anyone else either, since everyone else is at least as heavy.

cards.t: Hard Problems Requiring Their Own Proof
cards.f: In Bag of Tokens, when is it worth playing the most expensive remaining token face down?
cards.b: Only when we can't currently afford the cheapest token, we already have a score point to spend, and more than one token remains -- spending a point regains power to afford the cheap tokens.

cards.t: Hard Problems Requiring Their Own Proof
cards.f: In Meeting Scheduler, when a candidate overlap between two slots is too short, which slot's pointer advances, and why?
cards.b: The slot that ENDS EARLIER, because its own end is already the tightest constraint -- it can never overlap anything that comes after the other slot's start either.

cards.t: Hard Problems Requiring Their Own Proof
cards.f: What is the overlap formula used in Meeting Scheduler for two candidate slots?
cards.b: `[max(start1, start2), min(end1, end2)]`.

cards.f: What are the three questions to ask before committing to a two-pointer approach?
cards.b: (1) Do I have two meaningful positions? (2) Is there some ordering/monotonic property? (3) Can moving a pointer safely eliminate possibilities?

cards.f: A problem is about an unsorted array and needs to return original indices for a target-sum pair. Why not sort and use opposite-end pointers?
cards.b: Sorting would destroy the original indices that need to be returned. Use a HashMap instead.

cards.f: What problem signal points to Sliding Window instead of two pointers?
cards.b: A CONTIGUOUS subarray whose validity must be maintained as elements enter and leave a window, rather than two independent positions being narrowed toward each other.

cards.f: What is the recognition signal for fixed-gap pointers?
cards.b: "Find the element that is k positions behind/ahead of another element" -- keep two pointers a constant distance k apart and advance them together.

cards.f: What is the recognition signal for fast/slow pointers, and where is that pattern's full derivation covered?
cards.b: Linked-list midpoint or cycle detection (fast moves 2 steps per 1 slow step); the full derivation lives in the Linked List guide, not this one.

cards.f: What is the single universal test for whether two pointers is the right tool for a new problem?
cards.b: Can moving this pointer be PROVEN to eliminate possibilities that cannot contain the answer? If not, two pointers is the wrong tool.

cards.f: What complexity results from "sort + fixed pointer(s) + two pointers" in general, and why?
cards.b: Sorting costs O(n log n); the fixed-pointer(s) + L/R scan costs O(n) per fixed index combination, multiplied by n for each extra fixed index (3Sum: O(n^2), 4Sum: O(n^3)).

cards.f: Why does the source material discourage memorizing "sum small -> left++" as a template?
cards.b: Because templates memorized without the underlying elimination proof break the moment a problem's details shift slightly -- as both self-corrections in this guide (Two Sum II and 3Sum duplicate handling) show directly.

cards.f: What are the two fundamental pieces of a graph?
cards.b: Vertices (nodes, the things) and edges (the relationships between things). Graph = Nodes + Relationships.

cards.f: What is the "secretly a graph" recognition skill?
cards.b: Recognizing that many problems never using the word "graph" (grids, words, accounts, prerequisites) can still be modeled as nodes + edges.

cards.f: How do you model a grid/matrix problem as a graph?
cards.b: Each cell is a node; a cell's up-to-4 neighboring cells are its edges. This is why flood fill, mazes, and island problems are graph problems.

cards.f: What's the difference between a directed and undirected edge?
cards.b: Undirected: the relationship works both ways (A-B implies B-A). Directed: A -> B does NOT imply B -> A (e.g. prerequisites, follow relationships).

cards.f: What's the difference between weighted and unweighted graphs?
cards.b: Unweighted graphs only care whether a connection exists; weighted graphs attach a cost/value to each edge (distance, time, money).

cards.f: What is the degree of a node in an undirected graph?
cards.b: The number of edges touching that node.

cards.f: What's the difference between indegree and outdegree?
cards.b: Indegree = edges coming INTO a node; outdegree = edges going OUT of a node. Only meaningful for directed graphs.

cards.f: What is a connected component?
cards.b: A maximal group of nodes where every node can reach every other node through the graph -- "can reach" doesn't require a direct edge.

cards.f: Why is adjacency list usually the default graph representation?
cards.b: It only stores edges that actually exist: O(V+E) space, versus an adjacency matrix's O(V^2) space which wastes space on sparse graphs.

cards.f: When is an adjacency matrix the better representation?
cards.b: When you need O(1) lookup for "is there a direct edge between u and v?" -- useful for dense or small graphs.

cards.f: When is an edge list the best representation?
cards.b: When you need to process or sort edges globally, e.g. Kruskal's MST algorithm.

cards.f: How does one DFS call relate to a connected component?
cards.b: One DFS call started from an unvisited node completely consumes that node's entire connected component.

cards.f: How do you count connected components using DFS?
cards.b: Loop through every node; each time you find an unvisited node, start a new DFS and increment the component count.

cards.f: Why is "if DFS sees a visited node, there's a cycle" wrong for undirected graphs?
cards.b: Because DFS always sees its own parent as "already visited" when backtracking -- that's normal, not a cycle.

cards.f: What is the correct invariant for undirected cycle detection via DFS?
cards.b: If DFS encounters a visited neighbor that is NOT the current node's parent, that's a cycle.

cards.f: Why does seeing a visited, non-parent neighbor prove a cycle?
cards.b: It means there's already another route connecting the current DFS path back to that node -- two routes between the same pair of nodes is exactly a cycle.

cards.f: What is the bipartite graph invariant?
cards.b: Every edge must connect nodes of opposite colors when the graph is split into two groups via 2-coloring.

cards.f: How do you check if a graph is bipartite?
cards.b: BFS or DFS 2-coloring: assign a start node color 0, force every neighbor to the opposite color; if any edge connects two same-colored nodes, it's not bipartite.

cards.f: What's the connection between bipartite graphs and cycles?
cards.b: A graph is bipartite exactly when it contains no odd-length cycle. An odd cycle always creates a same-color contradiction when alternating colors.

cards.f: What kind of question does topological sort answer?
cards.b: "What order can these things be done in?" -- not reachability, but valid orderings under dependency constraints.

cards.f: What makes a node "safe to process first" in Kahn's algorithm?
cards.b: Having indegree 0 -- nothing depends on it being done first, so no prerequisite blocks it.

cards.f: In the graph A->C, B->C, C->D, which nodes are safe to process first?
cards.b: Both A and B -- both have indegree 0. (A common mistake is naming only one of them.)

cards.f: Does topological sort always produce a unique ordering?
cards.b: No -- multiple valid orderings usually exist whenever more than one node has indegree 0 at some point.

cards.f: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle?
cards.b: If it can't process every node (some nodes never reach indegree 0), those remaining nodes are part of a cycle.

cards.f: What are the three states in three-color DFS cycle detection?
cards.b: WHITE (never visited), GRAY (currently on the recursion stack), BLACK (fully processed, cannot lead back to the current stack).

cards.f: In three-color DFS, what does seeing a GRAY neighbor mean?
cards.b: The current DFS path has looped back onto itself -- a cycle. A BLACK neighbor is always safe (already proven acyclic).

cards.f: How does DFS-based topological sort work?
cards.b: Append a node to the result only after all its outgoing edges are fully explored (postorder), then reverse the final list.

cards.f: If a problem needs the lexicographically smallest valid topological order, what changes?
cards.b: Swap the plain queue of zero-indegree nodes for a min-heap.

cards.f: What's the recognition trigger for topological sort?
cards.b: Words like "prerequisite", "dependency", "before", "build order", "scheduling" -> directed graph -> topological sort / cycle detection.

cards.f: What problem is DSU specifically designed to solve?
cards.b: Efficiently answering "are these two nodes in the same group?" as relationships/edges arrive one at a time, without re-running DFS/BFS from scratch each time.

cards.f: What is the one-line mental model contrasting DFS/BFS and DSU?
cards.b: DFS/BFS explores an existing graph; DSU maintains connected components as relationships change.

cards.f: What does find(x) return?
cards.b: The representative (root) of the set containing x.

cards.f: How do you check if two nodes are in the same DSU group?
cards.b: Compare find(a) == find(b) -- never compare parent[a] == parent[b] directly, since parent only points one step up.

cards.f: What problem does path compression solve?
cards.b: Tall DSU chains make find() slow (many hops). Path compression makes every node on the path point directly at the root during find().

cards.f: What is the path compression line "parent[x] = find(parent[x])" actually doing?
cards.b: Finding the root recursively AND rewriting x's parent to that root on the way back out -- so future find() calls on that path are O(1).

cards.f: What is the union-by-size rule?
cards.b: Attach the smaller tree's root under the larger tree's root, to avoid building unnecessarily tall trees.

cards.f: How does union by rank differ from union by size?
cards.b: Union by rank tracks an approximate tree height instead of node count; attach the lower-rank root under the higher-rank root, incrementing rank only when merging equal-rank trees.

cards.f: What is the amortized time complexity of DSU with both path compression AND union by size/rank?
cards.b: O(alpha(n)) per operation, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function -- effectively constant for any practical input size.

cards.f: What is DSU's biggest limitation compared to DFS/BFS?
cards.b: DSU only tracks connectivity (same group or not) -- it can never answer "what is the shortest path?" or "what is the actual path?"

cards.f: When should you reach for DSU instead of DFS/BFS?
cards.b: When edges/relationships arrive dynamically one at a time and you repeatedly need "same group?" queries, or "does this edge create a cycle?"

cards.f: How do you count connected components with DSU?
cards.b: Start with n components; every successful union() reduces the count by 1.

cards.f: How does Redundant Connection use DSU?
cards.b: Process edges one at a time; the first edge whose union() call fails (already connected) is the redundant edge that would create a cycle.

cards.f: What two conditions make a graph a valid tree (Graph Valid Tree)?
cards.b: Exactly n-1 edges AND no cycle (every union() call succeeds).

cards.f: What is the key modeling trick in Accounts Merge?
cards.b: Model each email as a node; two accounts sharing an email get unioned together -- "shared identifier -> same component."

cards.f: What is the key modeling trick in Most Stones Removed?
cards.b: Model rows and columns (not stones) as DSU nodes; each stone connects its row-node to its column-node.

cards.f: What's the formula for the answer in Most Stones Removed?
cards.b: total stones - number of connected components (must leave at least one stone per component).

cards.f: Why is Number of Islands II a strong DSU use case?
cards.b: Land arrives one cell at a time and needs a running island count after each addition -- exactly the dynamic connectivity DSU is built for.

cards.f: What is the processing-order rule in Satisfiability of Equality Equations?
cards.b: Process every "==" constraint first (union), THEN check every "!=" constraint for a contradiction (same root despite claiming inequality).

cards.f: How do you compute the minimum operations to connect a network (Make Connected)?
cards.b: If there are fewer than n-1 cables, return -1. Otherwise the answer is (number of components - 1).

cards.f: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
cards.b: BFS explores strictly by increasing distance, so the first time it reaches any node is guaranteed to be via the fewest possible edges.

cards.f: Why does Dijkstra require non-negative edge weights?
cards.b: Its correctness relies on finalizing a node's distance the moment it's popped -- only safe because no future edge (all non-negative) can ever make it cheaper.

cards.f: What does the "if current_dist > dist[node]: continue" line in Dijkstra do?
cards.b: Skips a stale heap entry -- a worse (dist,node) pair pushed before a better route to that node was found.

cards.f: When should you use 0-1 BFS instead of Dijkstra?
cards.b: When every edge weight is exactly 0 or 1 -- a deque (push 0-weight to front, 1-weight to back) replaces the heap and is faster.

cards.f: Why does Bellman-Ford need up to V-1 relaxation passes?
cards.b: A shortest simple path has at most V-1 edges (more would repeat a vertex); each pass lets shortest-path info travel one more edge.

cards.f: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle?
cards.b: If a distance can still be improved on an extra pass beyond V-1, some reachable cycle must be making it artificially cheaper forever.

cards.f: What question does Floyd-Warshall answer that single-source algorithms don't?
cards.b: Shortest paths between EVERY pair of nodes at once, not just from one source.

cards.f: What is the core comparison in Floyd-Warshall's relaxation step?
cards.b: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) -- is routing through k cheaper than the current best?

cards.f: What is the shortest-path decision ladder, weight-type by weight-type?
cards.b: Unweighted -> BFS. 0/1 weights -> 0-1 BFS. Non-negative -> Dijkstra. Negative edges -> Bellman-Ford. All pairs -> Floyd-Warshall.

cards.f: What is a spanning tree?
cards.b: A subgraph that includes every vertex, stays connected, and has no cycle -- always exactly V-1 edges.

cards.f: How does MST differ from shortest path?
cards.b: Shortest path cares about one source and one destination; MST cares about connecting ALL vertices with minimum total edge weight.

cards.f: What is Kruskal's core rule?
cards.b: Sort edges cheapest-first; add an edge only if it connects two currently different components (checked via DSU).

cards.f: What is Prim's core rule?
cards.b: Grow one connected tree by repeatedly taking the cheapest edge from the current tree to any unvisited vertex, using a min-heap.

cards.f: What's the key difference between Dijkstra's and Prim's heap priority, even though the code looks similar?
cards.b: Dijkstra's priority is the TOTAL distance from the source; Prim's priority is just the weight of the ONE edge connecting a candidate node.

cards.f: What is the "virtual source" MST modeling trick?
cards.b: When each node can independently connect to a shared resource at some cost (e.g. build-a-well), add a virtual SOURCE node with that cost as an edge weight, turning it into ordinary MST.

cards.f: What are the three questions to ask for any "transform X into Y" problem?
cards.b: (1) What is a state? (2) When are two states connected? (3) Does each transition cost the same? If yes, it's BFS.

cards.f: How is Word Ladder modeled as a graph?
cards.b: Each word is a node; two words have an edge if they differ by exactly one character. Then it's unweighted shortest path -> BFS.

cards.f: When should you use bidirectional BFS?
cards.b: When both start and target are known and the branching factor is large -- search from both ends, always expanding the smaller frontier.

cards.f: In "The Maze" (LC 490), what is one BFS "edge"?
cards.b: A full roll until the ball hits a wall -- not a single cell step.

cards.f: In "Nearest Exit from Entrance in Maze," what's the easy-to-miss rule?
cards.b: The entrance cell itself is never counted as a valid exit, even though it sits on the border like a real exit would.

cards.f: What's the key insight for Cheapest Flights Within K Stops?
cards.b: dist[node] alone isn't enough info -- the state must become (node, number_of_edges_used), turning it into a K+1-round Bellman-Ford variant.

cards.f: Why must Cheapest Flights Within K Stops copy the distance array each round?
cards.b: Updating in place lets an improvement made earlier in the same round chain into a later edge in that same round, silently using more than the allowed number of edges.

cards.f: What is the general "expand the state" pattern?
cards.b: When a constraint (coupon, fuel, color just used, key collected) affects future moves, fold that constraint directly into the search state: dist[node][state] instead of dist[node].

cards.f: What's the difference between an Eulerian path and a Hamiltonian path?
cards.b: Eulerian = every EDGE exactly once. Hamiltonian = every VERTEX exactly once.

cards.f: Why doesn't naive greedy DFS solve Reconstruct Itinerary?
cards.b: It can pick an early destination that strands an edge, reachable from nowhere once the rest of the graph is exhausted.

cards.f: What is Hierholzer's algorithm's core rule?
cards.b: Finalize (append) a node only when it has no unused outgoing edges left, then reverse the final list.

cards.f: How is a character-ordering graph inferred from a sorted word list?
cards.b: Compare each pair of ADJACENT words; the first position where they differ gives one directed ordering edge between those two characters.

cards.f: Why only compare adjacent words, not every pair?
cards.b: Comparing every pair creates redundant edges; the ordering is already fully implied through the chain of adjacent comparisons.

cards.f: What invalid case does Alien Dictionary need to check explicitly (besides a cycle)?
cards.b: A longer word appearing before its own prefix (e.g. ["abc","ab"]) -- contradicts the rule that a prefix must sort first.

cards.f: What's the recognition chain for "how many groups are there?"
cards.b: groups -> connected components -> DFS/BFS (or DSU if edges arrive dynamically).

cards.f: What's the recognition chain when a problem "doesn't look like a graph at all"?
cards.b: Find the hidden STATE and TRANSITION, then apply BFS/DFS/Dijkstra to that state graph.

cards.f: Why is it dangerous to assume "I'm studying DSU, so this must be DSU"?
cards.b: Because many problems reuse the same graph but ask different questions requiring different tools (e.g. MST vs. shortest path on the same weighted graph) -- recognition must come from the question, not the current study topic.

cards.f: What is the difference between a subarray, a subsequence and a subset?
cards.b: Subarray = contiguous elements. Subsequence = order preserved but gaps allowed. Subset = any selection, order irrelevant. Most array patterns here (prefix sum, Kadane, sliding window, difference array) are about subarrays because contiguity allows a running summary.

cards.f: What is the one-question decision tree order for a new array problem?
cards.b: Contiguous range/subarray? -> Prefix Sum family. Need best contiguous sum -> Kadane. Range updates -> Difference Array. Info from both sides -> Prefix/Suffix. Values are indices -> Cyclic Sort. [start,end] pairs -> Sort + greedy. 2D -> Matrix. Rearrange in place -> In-place pointers. Otherwise -> Hashing fundamentals.

cards.f: What does prefix sum precompute, and what does it buy you?
cards.b: prefix[i] = sum of nums[0..i-1] (zero-padded). Any range sum becomes O(1): sum(l, r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]. Build is O(n) time/space.

cards.f: Why zero-pad the prefix array (prefix = [0, ...])?
cards.b: So sum(l, r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] works with no special case when l == 0.

cards.f: How does prefix sum extend to a 2D matrix?
cards.b: P[r][c] = sum of rectangle (0,0)..(r-1,c-1). Region sum = P[r2+1][c2+1] - P[r1][c2+1] - P[r2+1][c1] + P[r1][c1] (inclusion/exclusion: the overlapping corner is subtracted twice, so add it back once). LC 304.

cards.f: How does "count subarrays with sum K" become a hash lookup?
cards.b: Subarray (i+1..j) has sum prefix[j] - prefix[i]. We want that = K, so prefix[i] = prefix[j] - K. While scanning, ask "have I previously seen prefix - K?" and look it up in a map in O(1).

cards.f: Why must the prefix_count map start as {0: 1}?
cards.b: It records that a prefix sum of 0 existed before any element, so subarrays starting at index 0 can be detected. Without it, e.g. nums=[1,2], K=3 would miss [1,2].

cards.f: For the subarray-sum-K template, what order do the map operations go in per element?
cards.b: Update running prefix, look up count of (prefix - K) and add to the answer, THEN increment prefix_count[prefix]. Storing first could let a subarray of length 0 (K = 0) count itself.

cards.f: Counting subarrays vs longest subarray: what does the map store in each case?
cards.b: Counting: prefix -> frequency (every earlier occurrence is a different valid subarray). Longest: prefix -> EARLIEST index only (never overwrite), because the earliest start maximizes current_index - stored_index.

cards.f: Why must you never overwrite an existing entry in the longest-subarray-with-sum-K map?
cards.b: A later occurrence of the same prefix would give a shorter subarray. Keep the first index; only insert when prefix not in the map.

cards.f: How does LC 525 (Contiguous Array, equal 0s and 1s) reduce to prefix sums?
cards.b: Map 0 -> -1 and 1 -> +1. Equal counts means subarray sum == 0, i.e. a repeated prefix. Store the earliest index of each prefix with {0: -1} and maximize i - first[prefix].

cards.f: What changes for LC 974 (Subarray Sums Divisible by K)?
cards.b: (prefix[j] - prefix[i]) % k == 0 means prefix[j] % k == prefix[i] % k. Store remainder counts instead of prefix sums, start with {0: 1}. Python's % is already non-negative for positive k.

cards.f: What is the general pattern behind equal-0s-1s, equal-0s-1s-2s and similar problems?
cards.b: Multiple equality conditions -> represent the running state as a difference (or tuple of differences) -> same state seen before -> the subarray between them is valid. E.g. state = (count0 - count1, count1 - count2).

cards.f: Which signal words trigger Prefix Sum + HashMap?
cards.b: "subarray" + a sum/target condition + count / existence / longest. Thought process: current prefix -> what earlier prefix would make the difference K? -> prefix - K -> have I seen it? -> hash map.

cards.f: What problem shape suggests Prefix/Suffix preprocessing?
cards.b: An element needs information about everything to its left AND everything to its right. Preprocess left info in one pass and right info in another instead of rescanning for every index.

cards.f: How do you derive Product of Array Except Self without division?
cards.b: answer[i] = (product of everything left of i) x (product of everything right of i). Build left[i], build right[i], multiply. Collapse to O(1) extra space by storing left products in the output, then multiplying by a running right product in a reverse pass.

cards.f: Why is the division approach to Product of Array Except Self not robust?
cards.b: Any zero in the array breaks it: total = 0, so answer[i] = 0 / nums[i] raises ZeroDivisionError at the zero, and one-zero vs two-or-more-zeros needs hand-written special cases. Prefix/suffix products never divide, so zeroes need no special case.

cards.f: What is the core insight of the difference array?
cards.b: To add v to nums[l..r], do not touch every element. Record only where the change starts and stops: diff[l] += v and diff[r+1] -= v. A final running prefix sum over diff reconstructs the real array.

cards.f: Why does diff[r+1] -= v work?
cards.b: The prefix sum carries +v forward from index l onward; at index r+1 the -v cancels it exactly, so only l..r is affected.

cards.f: What is the relationship between prefix sum and difference array?
cards.b: They are inverses. Prefix Sum -> efficient range QUERIES on a static array. Difference Array -> efficient range UPDATES, with one prefix-sum pass at the end. Difference array = differences between consecutive elements.

cards.f: What is the Kadane recurrence and what does it mean?
cards.b: current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]). current is the best sum of a subarray ENDING at i: extend the previous segment, or throw it away and restart here (when the old segment is negative). best = max(best, current).

cards.f: Why is Kadane's algorithm "a very small DP"?
cards.b: dp[i] = max(nums[i], dp[i-1] + nums[i]) only needs dp[i-1], so the state compresses to one variable: O(n) time, O(1) space.

cards.f: Why must Kadane initialize current = best = nums[0] rather than 0?
cards.b: Initializing to 0 silently allows the empty subarray. On an all-negative array such as [-5,-2,-8,-1] it would report 0 instead of the correct -1.

cards.f: How do you solve Maximum Circular Subarray (LC 918)?
cards.b: Answer = max(ordinary Kadane max, total_sum - minimum_subarray_sum). The wrapped case removes the minimum subarray from the middle. Edge case: if every number is negative, total - min degenerates to the empty subarray, so return the ordinary Kadane result.

cards.f: Why does Maximum Product Subarray (LC 152) track both a max and a min?
cards.b: A very negative running product times a negative number becomes the biggest product. Track best and worst product ending here; swap them when the current number is negative.

cards.f: What is the connection between Kadane and prefix sums?
cards.b: A subarray i..j has sum prefix[j] - prefix[i-1], so max subarray = largest difference between a current prefix and an earlier prefix. Kadane packages that as a one-pass "best ending here" state. Prefix Sum: exact range sums matter. Kadane: best contiguous sum matters.

cards.f: What is the first move for almost every interval problem?
cards.b: Sort (by start for merging, by end for the greedy "keep the earliest finisher"), then do a single greedy scan. Ask: after sorting by what property does this become easy?

cards.f: How do two intervals A and B (A.start <= B.start) overlap?
cards.b: They overlap iff B.start <= A.end. Otherwise there is a gap and B starts a new group.

cards.f: How does Merge Intervals (LC 56) work?
cards.b: Sort by start. Keep a result list; if the next interval's start <= result[-1].end, extend result[-1].end = max(both ends); else append it. Invariant: only result[-1] can still overlap the current interval. O(n log n).

cards.f: How does Insert Interval (LC 57) avoid sorting?
cards.b: Input is already sorted, so three phases: append all intervals completely before the new one (end < new.start), merge all overlapping ones into the new interval (min of starts, max of ends), append the rest. O(n).

cards.f: How do you solve Non-overlapping Intervals (LC 435), the minimum removals problem?
cards.b: Greedy: sort by END. Keep an interval if start >= last kept end; otherwise it overlaps, so remove it (count += 1) and keep the one that ends earlier. Keeping the earliest finisher leaves the most room.

cards.f: What is the difference between Meeting Rooms (LC 252) and Meeting Rooms II (LC 253)?
cards.b: 252: can one person attend all meetings? Sort by start and check any start < previous end. 253: how many rooms are needed? That is the maximum number of simultaneously active meetings, computed with separately sorted starts and ends.

cards.f: How does the two-sorted-lists approach for Meeting Rooms II work?
cards.b: Sort all starts and all ends separately. Walk starts with a second pointer on ends: if next start < earliest unfinished end, rooms += 1 (track max); otherwise a room just freed up, so rooms -= 1 and advance the end pointer.

cards.f: What is the key signal for cyclic sort / index placement?
cards.b: The values themselves give you an index (values in 1..n or 0..n). The array can act as its own storage: value v belongs at index v-1 (or v).

cards.f: What is the fundamental swap operation in cyclic sort?
cards.b: While nums[i] is not at its correct index and the target slot doesn't already hold the same value: swap nums[i] with nums[correct]. Only advance i when nums[i] is already in place (or is a duplicate/out of range).

cards.f: Why must you NOT increment i right after a swap in cyclic sort?
cards.b: The value that just arrived at index i may also be misplaced and needs to be checked again immediately.

cards.f: Why is cyclic sort still O(n) despite the while loop inside the scan?
cards.b: Every swap puts at least one element permanently into its correct position, so total swaps <= n. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

cards.f: How do you solve First Missing Positive (LC 41)?
cards.b: The answer is in 1..n+1, so ignore values outside [1, n]. Place each v in 1..n at index v-1 (guarding against duplicates). Then the first index i where nums[i] != i+1 gives answer i+1; if all match, answer is n+1.

cards.f: How does cyclic sort handle Missing Number (LC 268) differently from the 1..n version?
cards.b: Values are 0..n, so value v belongs at index v (ignore v == n since no slot exists). After placement the first index with nums[i] != i is the missing number; if none, it's n.

cards.f: Why is LC 287 (Find the Duplicate Number) solved with Floyd's cycle detection instead of plain cyclic sort?
cards.b: LC 287 forbids modifying the array. Treating i -> nums[i] as a linked list turns the duplicate into a cycle; the cycle's entry point is the duplicate (find intersection, then restart one pointer from the start).

cards.f: When should you NOT use cyclic sort?
cards.b: When values have no natural value-to-index mapping (e.g. [-100, 57, 923, 18]). It requires values constrained to 1..n or 0..n. HashSet costs O(n) space; index placement gets O(1) space.

cards.f: How do you rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place?
cards.b: Transpose (swap matrix[i][j] and matrix[j][i] for j > i), then reverse every row. Counterclockwise: transpose then reverse the columns instead.

cards.f: Why does in-place transpose loop j from i+1 instead of 0?
cards.b: Each pair (i,j)/(j,i) must be swapped exactly once; iterating both triangles would swap twice and undo the work. Only works in place for square matrices.

cards.f: How does Spiral Matrix (LC 54) manage traversal?
cards.b: Four shrinking boundaries top, bottom, left, right: go right along top, down along right, left along bottom, up along left, shrinking each boundary after its side. Guard the third and fourth sides with if top <= bottom / if left <= right so a single row or column isn't visited twice.

cards.f: What is the O(1)-space trick for Set Matrix Zeroes (LC 73)?
cards.b: Use row 0 and column 0 as marker storage for "zero this row/col", with two booleans remembering whether row 0 and column 0 originally contained a zero. Mark first (scanning rows/cols 1..n), apply marks to the interior, and only THEN zero row 0 / col 0 using the saved flags.

cards.f: Why must Set Matrix Zeroes apply the row-0/col-0 flags last?
cards.b: Row 0 and column 0 are being reused as markers, so zeroing them early would corrupt markers that haven't been read yet.

cards.f: When is a matrix problem NOT an array-manipulation problem?
cards.b: When cells represent connectivity (0 = empty, 1 = occupied, neighbors are edges). Then it is grid BFS/DFS (regions, paths), a different toolbox. Matrix manipulation is an array problem; matrix connectivity is a graph problem.

cards.f: What is the read/write pointer pattern for in-place array problems?
cards.b: slow = next write position, fast = scanner reading every element. Copy nums[fast] to nums[slow] and advance slow only when the element should be kept. After the loop nums[:slow] is the answer.

cards.f: How does Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (LC 26) use the pattern?
cards.b: Sorted, so duplicates are adjacent. slow tracks the last unique element written; for fast from 1: if nums[fast] != nums[fast-1] then nums[slow] = nums[fast]; slow += 1. Return slow.

cards.f: How does Move Zeroes (LC 283) preserve order?
cards.b: Write every non-zero value forward with slow, then fill nums[slow:] with zeroes. Order of non-zero elements is preserved because fast scans left to right.

cards.f: What is partitioning and where else does it appear?
cards.b: Separating an array by a condition (negative | non-negative, < pivot | >= pivot). left scans for an element belonging right, right scans for one belonging left, swap. It is exactly the partition step of QuickSort.

cards.f: How does the reversal algorithm rotate an array right by k in O(1) extra space (LC 189)?
cards.b: k %= n; reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n-k elements.

cards.f: What is the difference between a HashSet and a HashMap in problem-solving terms?
cards.b: HashSet answers "do I have this?" (existence only). HashMap answers "what information do I have about this?" (count, index, group). If you only need existence, a map storing extra data is wasted work.

cards.f: What are the seven big hashing patterns?
cards.b: 1 Frequency (value -> count), 2 Existence (HashSet), 3 Seen-before (value -> seen), 4 Index tracking (value -> index), 5 Complement lookup (needed value -> lookup), 6 Grouping (canonical key -> group), 7 Prefix + HashMap (prefix state -> count/index).

cards.f: For index tracking, when do you store the first vs the latest index?
cards.b: Depends on the objective: for the LONGEST subarray you want the EARLIEST occurrence (maximizes current_index - earliest_index). Don't memorize "always first index"; ask what the index needs to optimize.

cards.f: How does Two Sum (LC 1) use complement lookup?
cards.b: For each num compute needed = target - num; if needed is in seen return its index and i; otherwise store seen[num] = i. Order matters: look up the complement THEN store, so the same element isn't used twice. O(n) average.

cards.f: How does the complement pattern generalize beyond Two Sum?
cards.b: Only the expression changes: target sum -> needed = target - current; target difference -> needed = current +/- target; XOR target -> needed = current XOR target. Same reasoning every time.

cards.f: What is a canonical key and how does Group Anagrams (LC 49) use one?
cards.b: Objects in the same category must map to the same representation. For anagrams the sorted string works ("eat" and "tea" -> "aet"); a 26-length count tuple is a faster O(n*k) alternative. Then groups[key].append(word).

cards.f: How does Intersection of Two Arrays II (LC 350) handle duplicates?
cards.b: Count one array; walk the other, and each time an element's count is still positive, append it to the answer and decrement its count. This limits repeats to the minimum count across both arrays.

cards.f: What is the trick for Encode and Decode Strings (LC 271)?
cards.b: Length-prefix each string: "<len>#<string>". The decoder always knows how many raw characters to consume next, so no delimiter escaping is needed even if a string contains '#'.

cards.f: What question should you ask instead of "use a hashmap?" when combining arrays and hashing?
cards.b: "What information would I want to remember while scanning the array?" Two Sum -> previous value, Contains Duplicate -> seen set, Top K -> frequency, Longest Consecutive -> fast existence checks, Subarray Sum K -> previous prefix sums.

cards.f: How does Longest Consecutive Sequence (LC 128) reach O(n)?
cards.b: Put all numbers in a set. Only start counting a sequence from a number with NO predecessor (num - 1 not in the set), then walk num+1, num+2... Every number belongs to exactly one walk, so total work is O(n).

cards.f: How do you solve Top K Frequent Elements (LC 347)?
cards.b: Two sub-problems: build a frequency map (Counter), then keep a min-heap of size k of (count, value): push each pair and pop the smallest when size > k. O(n log k) time. (Bucket sort by frequency gives O(n).)

cards.f: How does Boyer-Moore voting solve Majority Element (LC 169) in O(1) space?
cards.b: Keep a candidate and a count. If count == 0 pick the current number as candidate; matching numbers count += 1, others count -= 1. The majority (> n/2 times) outnumbers all others combined, so it always survives the cancellation.

cards.f: How does Minimum Size Subarray Sum (LC 209) combine arrays with sliding window?
cards.b: All values are positive, so growing the right pointer only increases the sum and shrinking the left only decreases it. Expand right, while sum >= target shrink left and record the minimal length. That monotonicity makes shrink-while-valid correct.

cards.f: How do you count distinct elements in every window of size k?
cards.b: Frequency map for a fixed window: increment on entry, decrement on exit, and DELETE the key when its count hits zero so len(freq) always equals the number of distinct values in the window.

cards.f: Signal -> pattern: "sum of every subarray equal to k"?
cards.b: Prefix Sum + HashMap.

cards.f: Signal -> pattern: "add value to every element in [l, r], many updates"?
cards.b: Difference Array.

cards.f: Why would the Meeting Rooms II sweep sort starts and ends into two SEPARATE arrays?
cards.b: The question is the maximum number of meetings active at one instant, which only needs the relative order of all starts against all ends. Sorting the (start, end) pairs together would lose that cross-interval ordering.

cards.f: What is the meta-pattern behind nearly all of Arrays & Hashing?
cards.b: Ask what information from the past would let you solve the current position in O(1), then store exactly that (a prefix, a running max, a count, an index, a canonical key).
